extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners evaluating prior art under the AIA
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining what constitutes prior art and applicable exceptions under the America Invents Act (AIA) 35 U.S.C. 102, including how to determine effective filing dates, categories of prior art (patented, printed publication, public use, on sale, otherwise available), and applicable statutory exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[A] the subject matter disclosed was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclosure that otherwise qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) is not prior art if the subject matter was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor. See MPEP discussion of exceptions; examiner should apply when the reference is a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or WIPO published application that was filed/published before the claimed invention's effective filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[B] the subject matter disclosed had, before such subject matter was effectively filed under subsection (a)(2), been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter disclosed directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor;"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject matter in the reference had already been publicly disclosed by the inventor (or someone who derived it from the inventor) before the reference was effectively filed, the reference may be excepted as prior art under 102(b)(2)(B). See MPEP § 2154 discussion and cross-reference to 2153.02 and 717.01(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C)
rubrics_metrics.description: "[C] the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common ownership or obligation to assign can prevent a U.S. patent, publication, or WIPO application from being prior art under 102(a)(2). Compare to pre-AIA 103(c); see MPEP § 2154.02(b) for differences and the tests for common ownership/assignment obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Filing Date of the Claimed Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA defines the term "effective filing date" for a claimed invention as the earliest of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or the application for the patent containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application for which the patent or application is entitled to a right of priority or the benefit of an earlier filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, 121, 365, or 386 (see 35 U.S.C. 100(i)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When examining applications subject to AIA 102, the effective filing date is the actual U.S. application filing date unless one of these situations applies: (A) continuation/divisional with 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c)/386(c) satisfied (effective date = earliest in line); (B) continuation-in-part — claims not supported in parent get new application's filing date while fully supported claims have parent's date; (C) proper claim to a provisional under 119(e) — claims fully supported by provisional have provisional filing date; (D) foreign priority under 119(a)-(d), 365(a)/(b), 386(a)/(b) — effective date = foreign priority date if adequately supported. Also: national-stage and international filing date rules (PCT/371, Hague design) apply as discussed in referenced MPEP sections. The one-year grace period in AIA 102(b)(1) is measured from the filing date of any U.S. or foreign patent application to which benefit/priority is claimed, differing from pre-AIA measurement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim determination of effective filing date and application-by-application determination of AIA applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date of a claimed invention is determined on a claim-by-claim basis (different claims in the same application may have different effective filing dates). However, whether pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 or AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 applies is determined on an application-by-application basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must evaluate effective filing dates for each claim separately (see MPEP § 2133.01 discussion of continuation-in-part issues). In contrast, applicability of pre-AIA or AIA law is decided for the whole application (see MPEP §§ 2151 and 2159). Note also that under AIA it is no longer possible to 'swear behind' certain prior art via 37 CFR 1.131 (antedating) because AIA 102 focuses on effective filing dates rather than invention date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patented (35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)) — patent as prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent of a claimed invention will preclude a subsequent patent if the patent predates the effective filing date of the claimed invention. For purposes of 102(a)(1), the applicable date of a patent is the grant date, except where the patent was secret as of the date rights were awarded (then the date it was made available to the public applies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a patent describes (even if it does not claim) the claimed invention and was made available to the public on its grant date, that grant date is the prior-art date. A U.S. patent that issues after the claimed invention's effective filing date and is not available under 102(a)(1) may still be prior art under 102(a)(2). See MPEP § 2126 for secret-patent issues and In re Ekenstam/In re Carlson for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Described in a Printed Publication (anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)/(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: To anticipate, a prior art printed publication (patent, published application, or other printed publication) must: (1) disclose 'each and every element of the invention' either explicitly or inherently, with the elements 'arranged or combined in the same way as in the claim'; and (2) enable a person of ordinary skill in the art to make the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AIA does not change the extent required for a prior-art document to 'describe' a claimed invention for anticipation. There is no requirement that the prior art meet the 'how to use' aspect of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). For anticipation it is sufficient that one species or embodiment is described/enabled even if the claim is broader (see Vas-Cath v. Mahurkar and related cases). Prior art that does not meet anticipatory description may still be used in an obviousness rejection for what it would reasonably have made known to a person of ordinary skill. Case law examples: In re Gleave, Eli Lilly v. Zenith, Net MoneyIN v. VeriSign, In re Bond; enablement cases include Impax Labs., In re LeGrice; anticipatory-species cases include Vas-Cath, In re Lukach.

rubrics_metrics.name: In Public Use (35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use rejections may be based on uses anywhere in the world; the public use must occur before the effective filing date and must make the invention available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under AIA there is no geographic limitation. Public use that invalidates a patent generally falls into uses that were (1) accessible to the public, or (2) commercially exploited. Whether a use is public may depend on who made the use; an inventor's own prior commercial use, even if kept secret, may bar patentability under some circumstances. Showing an invention to another who is 'under no limitation of confidentiality' can create a public use. If an examiner becomes aware of a potentially public use, the examiner should require the applicant to provide information showing the use did not make the invention accessible to the public. Pre-AIA case law (Invitrogen, Woodland Trust, American Seating) provides background on tests of accessibility and confidentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: On Sale (35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: On sale rejections may be based on sales or offers for sale regardless of where they occurred; the phrase 'on sale' is treated the same as in pre-AIA 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-AIA law (Pfaff v. Wells Elecs.) indicates patentability is barred if the invention was (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale not primarily for experimental purposes, and (2) ready for patenting. Contract/commercial-law principles apply to determine whether a sale/offer occurred. The enablement inquiry does not apply to whether an invention is "on sale" under pre-AIA law, and AIA retains the same meaning. Under Helsinn (2019), a sale to a third party who is obligated to keep the invention confidential can still qualify as prior art under 102(a). Examiners should consider evidence of sales activity irrespective of location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Otherwise Available to the Public (35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A catch-all provision: a claimed invention is not entitled to a patent if it was 'otherwise available to the public' before its effective filing date; the focus is whether the disclosure was 'available to the public' rather than the means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of availability include a student thesis in a university library, poster display or information disseminated at a scientific meeting, subject matter in a laid-open patent application or patent, documents electronically posted on the Internet, or commercial transactions that do not constitute a sale under the UCC. Even if a disclosure is not a printed publication, printed patent, or a sale, it may still be prior art if made sufficiently available to the public (see In re Cronyn, In re Klopfenstein, Voter Verified, In re Lister, Group One v. Hallmark).

rubrics_metrics.name: No Requirement of 'By Others' under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A key difference from pre-AIA 102(a) is that under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) there is no requirement that the prior art relied on be 'by others'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any prior art falling under 102(a)(1) need not be by another to be potentially available prior art. However, disclosures made one year or less before the effective filing date by the inventor or a joint inventor (or someone who obtained the subject matter from them) may fall within exceptions under 102(b)(1). Examiners should therefore consider 102(b)(1) exceptions where inventor-originated disclosures are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions as Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions by the applicant (in the specification or during prosecution) identifying the work of another as 'prior art' are treated as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such admissions can be relied upon for both anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of whether the admitted prior art would otherwise qualify as statutory prior art under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102. See Riverwood Int'l Corp. v. R.A. Jones & Co., Constant v. AMD, and MPEP § 2129 for discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'Disclosure' (generic usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office treats the term 'disclosure' as a generic expression intended to encompass the documents and activities enumerated in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a) (being patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, on sale, otherwise available to the public, or being described in U.S. patents/publications/WIPO applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although AIA 102(a) does not use the term 'disclosure' and AIA does not define it, the MPEP uses 'disclosure' generically. Examiners should interpret 'disclosure' to include all enumerated categories and apply the relevant tests for each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining Whether To Apply 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) or 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should first consider whether a reference qualifies as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) and then determine if any exceptions in 102(b)(1) apply. Separately, they should consider whether the reference qualifies under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2) and then determine if any exceptions in 102(b)(2) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 102(a)(1) consider patents, printed publications, public use, on-sale, and otherwise-available disclosures that predate the claim's effective filing date; the activity need not occur in the U.S. If a reference is by the inventor or derived from the inventor and was made one year or less before the effective filing date, consider 102(b)(1)(A)/(B) exceptions (see MPEP §§ 2153.01(a), 2153.01(b), 2153.02). Under 102(a)(2), U.S. patents, U.S. patent application publications, and PCT published applications are prior art if their filing/effective filing date is before the claim's effective filing date; use 35 U.S.C. 102(d) to determine when subject matter was "effectively filed." Then consider 102(b)(2)(A)-(C) exceptions. See MPEP §§ 2152, 2154, 717.01, and cited sections for procedural application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation vs Obviousness — differing description/enablement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation under 102(a)(1)/(a)(2), a prior art document must describe and enable all elements of the claim as arranged in the claim; for obviousness under 103, a disclosure may be cited for what it would reasonably have made known to a person of ordinary skill even if it does not anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The written-description/enablement needed to anticipate is less than that required to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for supporting a claim's entire scope: a single species disclosure can anticipate a broader claim. However, a reference lacking the requisite anticipatory description may still support an obviousness rejection for its teachings. See case law distinctions: Rasmussen v. SmithKline Beecham, Vas-Cath, Gleave, Schoenwald, Schering, Impax, and related MPEP discussion.
